name: The Powell household — a name from the post office's letter lists
head: powell_geo_n

arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE RETURN, NOT AN ARRIVAL. The office's list of letters uncalled-for is a RETURN — its statement of what was still unclaimed on ONE day — and the paper reprinted one return over as many consecutive issues as it took, so the bound is dated by the return of 1 April 1834 and not by the issue it was read in (T-0425). Somebody was writing to this name at Chicago by 1834-04-01 and at no stated time before it; nothing says when they came. The date lines the printings set, and how they were weighed, stand beside this rule in tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py.

arrival_year.note: DRAWN, NOT READ. The household's arrival block holds a BOUND — somebody was here by 1834-04-01 and no source says when they came — so the year is drawn from the arrival years the known layer records, truncated at that bound and renormalised. It says what a household of this bound most likely was, and nothing whatever about this household.

origin.note: DRAWN FROM A SURVIVORSHIP SAMPLE. No source says where this household came from. The region is drawn from the birthplaces of the seventy Old Settlers who registered an arrival at or before 1835 — a self-selected roll set down forty-four years later that over-represents the men who stayed and prospered, as the town model's own open questions say. It is the only origin distribution this project holds and this value is drawn from it, not measured.

reason_for_coming.note: ARGUED FROM THE SEASON AND NOTHING ELSE. No trade is recorded for this household and no source says why it came; the only thing the evidence gives is when it was here by. This states the draws that were operating in that season and chooses among them nowhere. Which of these draws brought this household is not recorded, and no committed source apportions the town between them.

persons.name: Geo. N. Powell

later_occupation.note: NONE RECORDED FOR 1835 — AND A TRADE IS RECORDED FOR 1839. This is a POINTER at `directories.people[].occupation_later` on this same record, derived by `tools/qualify_later_trades.py` and holding nothing that block does not already say. It is not a claim about the scene date: the 1835 occupation above still reads `none_recorded`, its grade has not moved, and no premises has been sought on the strength of it, because a directory of 1839 is evidence about 1839. It is written because the field a reader consults was asserting an absence this file contradicts three lines further down, and "no trade anywhere" and "no trade in the scene window, one printed 1839" are not the same fact (T-0693).

occupation.note: No source records an occupation for this person. A list of uncalled-for letters prints a name and no trade, and this pass will not read one in.

persons.note: GRADED BY THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER — rule G2e, applied 2026-09-04. This identity is inferred because that rung fired on the civic and press rows recorded on this card, which the resident-research corpus does not read. This programme's letter-list rule of 2026-09-02 would call it a projected resident on the absence of a research row; it is superseded here, and a no-find in one corpus is not a finding about another (T-0822). KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Geo. N. Powell { HE su' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 April 1834, column 2 — dated 1834-04-01. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1).

resident_research.summary: No reliable record in the reviewed repository corpus, exact/variant searches, 1839/1843 Chicago directories, and targeted regional/local histories could be tied to this person by more than the recorded postal name. This is a documented no-corroboration result, not evidence that the person did not exist.

roles.note: A TRADE PRINTED AGAINST THIS NAME IN A LATER VOLUME, and this row says which year rather than leaving it to a pointer (T-0693, carried here by tools/derive_resident_roles.py). `role` is null because the directory's wording has not been adjudicated into the closed vocabulary — the printing is what the source gives and the printing is what is kept. T-1254 is where the controlled term is ruled on. It is not a claim about 1835-07-01 and never becomes one: the year is 1839.

basis.note: Drawn from the 1840 Chicago schedule's column 'free white males 30 under 40', one of its male bands, conditioned on `named_on_a_roll_15_and_over` because the person is named in their own right on any other roll this layer was minted from - a letter list, a subscription, a court docket, a trade notice - or carries a role, a trade, a marriage or a parenthood.

replaceable_by.match: a source that states this person's age, their birth year, or an interval either can be read out of

age_band.note: AN AGE BAND, NEVER A YEAR. No source this project holds bears on when this person was born, so the band is drawn from the only committed sex by age distribution the project has - the 1840 Chicago schedule, five years after the scene and a town twice the size - seeded by this person's own id ('powell_geo_n:age_bands_1840'). AND THE CONDITIONING IS THE MODEL'S, NOT A SOURCE'S: that a roll naming a person in their own right names somebody 15 or over. The 1840 schedule counts a child as a tally inside a household and never as a correspondent; 15 rather than 20 because an apprentice or a journeyman stands on a trade roll. No source states this rule. No exact year is written, because a year drawn from a decadal band would read as a record of a birth.

sex_basis.note: 'Geo.' IS THE PERIOD CONTRACTION OF George, and every expansion of it attested in this project is a man's name — so the contraction settles the sex without settling which name was contracted. The table is data/research/residents/forename_sex.json.

research_note: MINTED FROM THE LETTER LISTS (T-0378, T-0379). THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER, NOT AN ARGUMENT: every other record here argues for a household, and this one argues for a PERSON. `data/residents/` cannot carry a person outside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing — one member, no dwelling, no division, no trade, no family, no arrival beyond the paper's bound. tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py derives the set and prints every refusal, `--gate` proves no record here gained a roof, a trade or a second member, and docs/LIBERTIES.md L214 carries the change of scale.

surname_collision.refusal: the town already names a Powell
surname_collision.note: A COLLISION SAID, NOT ACTED ON. Run against the tree as it stands, this pass would not MINT this card: refusal 7 — 'the town already names a Powell' — lands on it, because Reuben Powell (hh_powell_reuben) already holds the family name Powell. The owner ruled on 2026-09-18 (T-0660, option (c)) that refusals 7 and 8 are MINT-TIME rules: they decide whether a new household may be minted on a family name the town already spends, and they do not un-mint one that already stands. So this record is not retired, its id is not redirected at anybody, the town's population does not move, and the research row and directory matches it carries are not stranded on a retirement nothing draws. What has changed is that the collision is legible: a reader sees both cards and why both are here. REFUSAL 7 IS NOT A CLAIM THAT TWO RECORDS ARE ONE PERSON — it is the precedence rule between this pass and the ones above it, which give a man the papers gave a trade the family name a letter list only spells. Two of the collisions this reading uncovered are two different men. The pass's `rank()` is unchanged and the cohort is not re-derived; that was option (b)'s cost and the ruling declined to pay it. The derivation behind this block, both readings side by side, is docs/RESEARCH/letter-list-surname-collisions.md.

old_settler_deaths.the_header_admission:
Names, places * , dates, and ages at death
of some of Chicago's Old Settlers, prior to 1843, and other well - known citizens who arrived after 1843, together
with others prominently connected with Illinois history:
old_settler_deaths.note: LATER EVIDENCE OF A DEATH, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. Fergus's 1843 directory (1896) prints an obituary list of old settlers, and one of its entries meets somebody of this name. THE HEADER OF THE LIST IS QUOTED ABOVE, and it is the limit the whole reading turns on. It does not mean the person was in Chicago in 1835, and it does not mean they arrived before 1843 — the list's own header, quoted above, says it also names citizens who arrived later and others merely 'prominently connected with Illinois history'. A match means one thing: a name in the 1835 layer and a name in this list agree on surname and first initial, and the list gives that name a death date and an age. The date and the interval are the payload. Whatever is carried is carried as evidence of a DEATH and of an interval the birth falls in, never as an 1835 fact and never as a grade. T-0513 consolidates and T-0514/T-0515 apply; this file changes no record. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. A death notice printed in 1896 says a person of this name died on a day; under the ratified ladder (T-0513) that is later evidence about a DEATH, and it is never an 1835 residence. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. WHAT THIS PASS RULED ONTO THIS HOUSEHOLD, named so the ruling can be found again: each volume below is followed by the printed entries it set against this person and the status the crosswalk ruled them at — a single entry carries what its own `could_carry` declares, and an ambiguous or contested match carries nothing and is shown so that the silence is legible. powell_geo_n, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 — f1839_e1187 (a single entry).

occupation_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this trade against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Powell, George N., tavern-keeper, Milwaukee ave'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.

back_projection.note: REFUSED, AND THE REFUSAL IS THE RECORD. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints an address against this name in 1839 and this pass will not carry it back to 1835. The 1835 record prints no trade for this person, so there is no 1835 business for a later door to position. Minting one out of a directory printed after the scene date is the one thing this pass may never do. A refusal is written here rather than dropped so that a later run can see the address was read and ruled on, not missed (docs/ADDRESS-BACK-PROJECTION.md, clause 1).
